chunks.text: Karanj (Pongamia pinnata), also called Indian beech or Millettia pinnata in some older classifications, is a legume tree in the pea family Fabaceae. It was first described by Linnaeus in 1753 as Cytisus pinnatus and later moved through several genera before being restored as the sole member of its own genus, Pongamia. It is native across tropical and temperate Asia — from India through Southeast Asia to Japan — and into northeastern Australia and the Pacific, and has since naturalised widely across Africa, the Caribbean and other tropical regions since the 19th century. The tree grows 15-25 m tall with a trunk 50-80 cm across and grey-brown, smooth-to-fissured bark, and has an expansive canopy that casts dense shade. Its compound (imparipinnate) leaves start soft and burgundy-tinged before maturing to glossy dark green, and after 3-4 years the tree produces small, fragrant white, purple and pink flowers followed by thick-walled seed pods, each usually holding one or two oily, brownish-red seeds. It is strikingly hardy: seedlings tolerate salinity up to 12-19 dS/m (surviving even 32.5 dS/m), the tree can withstand total submergence for extended periods, and it copes with temperatures from just below 0°C to about 50°C on 500-2,500 mm of annual rainfall.

Karanj seeds contain 27-39% oil, roughly half of it oleic acid; the pressed 'pongamia oil' has long been used as lamp oil, in soapmaking and as a lubricant, and has become one of India's most researched biodiesel feedstocks because it grows on marginal land unsuited to food crops. The oil is bitter and can cause nausea if eaten raw, owing to compounds like karanjin and pongamol, but in traditional medicine the fruits, sprouts and seeds have been used for various ailments, and the bark has reportedly been used to neutralise certain fish venoms. The wood is attractively grained but splits easily, limiting it mostly to firewood, fence posts and tool handles; the bark yields a black gum, and flowers are sometimes used as compost. Ecologically, karanj's deep taproot and its nitrogen-fixing root nodules (formed in partnership with Bradyrhizobium bacteria) make it valuable for stabilising sand dunes and controlling soil erosion, which is part of why it is so often planted along Indian roads and coastlines despite poor soil. Byproducts of oil extraction have also been studied as animal feed, containing up to 30% protein.
